title: Word Squares
statement:
You are given an array `words` of distinct lowercase strings that all have the same length `L`. A **word square** is a list of `L` words written one per row, top to bottom, so that the grid reads the same across and down: for every `k` from `0` to `L - 1`, row `k` is equal to column `k` (the string formed by the `k`-th letters of the rows, read from the top).

Return every word square that can be built from `words`. The same word may be used in more than one row of a square. The squares may be returned in any order, but the words inside each square must be listed from the top row down. Return an empty list when no square can be built.
constraints: All words[i] have the same length
words[i] consists of only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every list of `L` words and checking the grid costs about n^L checks. But the rows are not free: once rows `0` to `r - 1` are placed, column `r` already shows its first `r` letters, and row `r` must equal column `r`. So the next row must start with a known prefix. Indexing every word under each of its prefixes turns "which words could go here?" into one map lookup, and backtracking only ever tries words that fit.

## Approach

1. Let `size` be the word length. For every word and every prefix length `0` to `size - 1`, add the word to `byPrefix` under that prefix (the empty prefix lists every word).
2. Grow `square` one row at a time in `build`. When it holds `size` rows, it is complete: store a copy in `result`.
3. Otherwise the next row index is `row = square.length`. Read column `row` of the rows so far into `prefix` by taking `word[row]` from each placed word.
4. For each word in `candidates = byPrefix.get(prefix)`, push it, recurse, and pop it to try the next one.

## Example 1, step by step

`size = 4`. Row 0 may be any word. With `"area"` the next prefix is `"r"` and with `"lead"` it is `"e"`: no word starts with either, so both die at once. With `"wall"`, row 1 needs prefix `"a"` → `"area"`; row 2 needs `"l" + "e" = "le"` → `"lead"`; row 3 needs `"l" + "a" + "d" = "lad"` → `"lady"`, and the square is complete. `"lady"` reaches `"area"` but then needs `"de"`, which fails. `"ball"` follows the same path as `"wall"`. The result is `[["wall","area","lead","lady"],["ball","area","lead","lady"]]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n·L²) to build the index, plus O(L) for each partial square the search visits; every visited state is consistent, so no hopeless word is tried past its own row.
- Space: O(n·L²) for the prefix keys and lists, O(L) for the recursion and `square`, plus the output.

## Pitfalls

- A square has exactly `size` rows; stopping at any other count builds the wrong shape.
- Words may repeat inside a square (Example 2 uses `"baba"` twice), so do not mark words as used.
- Store a copy (`[...square]`): `square` keeps changing as the search backtracks.
- The prefix comes from column `row` (`word[row]` of each placed word), not from the last row.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `size` | the word length, which is also the number of rows |
| `byPrefix` | maps each prefix to the words that start with it |
| `square` | the rows placed so far |
| `row` | index of the row being filled |
| `prefix` | column `row` read from the placed rows; the next word must start with it |
| `candidates` | the words that start with `prefix` |
| `result` | every completed square |
